title: Major tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to fears of AI slowdown
content: Hundreds of billions of dollars in market value has been wiped from major tech firms in the US and Asia in a stock market rout after the US midterm elections sparked concerns of a slowdown in artificial intelligence development. Shares in firms across the tech and AI sectors plummeted following Democratic wins after election campaigns run on slowing AI. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite index closed down by more than 5.5%, losing an estimated $2.5tn (£1.9tn) in market value, according to Dow Jones data, while other key US stock indexes also saw big losses in their worst days since 2025. The sell-off comes on top of broader concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off. In Asia, tech-heavy indexes fell sharply on Friday morning as firms that make the computer chips and other equipment that power AI saw their shares slide. The Nikkei 225 in Japan was 6% lower in early trading as shares in memory chip maker Kioxia lost over 12.6% and rival Tokyo Electron slipped by 9.5%. South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix fell by more than 11.5%, while Samsung was down by nearly 10%. The sell-off in Seoul sent the Kospi index plunging more than 8.5%, triggering a so-called circuit breaker, a mechanism that temporarily halts trading to curb panic selling. Taiwan's Taiex dropped by more than 8.3%, with chipmaking giant TSMC falling by nearly 8.5%. It marks a "continuation of worries" over the level of spending on AI infrastructure, said MarketWatch chips analyst Britney Nguyen. Democrats in races across the US campaigned to slow the growth of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology. They won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of President Donald Trump's presidency. Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector. In a social media post, Trump blamed the slide on his political opponents. "The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election," he said. "Remember, it wasn't Republicans, it was Dumocrats. Do not fear, however, we will soon, one way or the other, be BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!" Some Democrats have argued that AI has grown too big without any safeguards or oversight and have promised, with their new power in Congress, to change that. "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future. NATIONAL DATA CENTER MORATORIUM NOW," Democrat Senator Bernie Sanders said in a post on X on Thursday. Shares in companies heavily exposed to AI data centres, including crucial chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers, fell sharply on Thursday, highlighting investor concerns that had already been growing. Nvidia shares slid more than 9%, knocking more than $400bn off the firm's market value. Other chipmakers also suffered, with AMD and Micron both dropping by more than 17%. Intel shares also dropped, down 10.3%, while memory card maker SanDisk plunged more than 22%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks the performance of 30 of the largest companies involved in semiconductor production, fell by more than 12%. Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value on Thursday. Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday night. In total, the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, have shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day. The stock falls also hit other major US stock indexes. The S&P 500 index fell by 4.4% by the end of trading, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average erased gains made on Wednesday to close down more than 3.4%. The Nasdaq Composite fall was so large it is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high. Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said the steep sell-off on the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 was sending shockwaves into other markets. "Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard," she said. "Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction." Greater scrutiny of data centre approvals, and their impact on the environment and electricity bills could delay projects and raise costs across the industry, said Charu Chanana, Chief Investment Strategist at Saxo. While both political parties are keen to ensure the US' dominance in the technology, "there is a difference between supporting AI development and allowing infrastructure to expand at any cost or pace," she said. Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms. OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board. "A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California on Wednesday evening. Meta's president Dina Powell McCormick said that the industry needed to put more effort into selling AI as a good idea. "I think we need to double and triple down on telling the story," she told the WSJ conference. Alongside the immediate impacts of the US mid-term elections, some investors have become concerned that AI shares could be in a bubble that is due a correction . With additional reporting from Lily Jamali

title: Food, fuel and taxes – can the Democrats actually make life cheaper?
content: Two business owners, half a country apart, want the same thing for different reasons. In Texas, Kim Hanks, who owns Tillies, a hotel, restaurant and spa business near Austin, says rising grocery and fuel costs are forcing her to raise wages for her 300 staff. "It's been such a moving target for us on affordability," she told the BBC World Service. In Indiana, Danny Reynolds, who runs Stephenson's of Elkhart, a clothing and bridalwear store, simply wants Washington to get its act together. "My hope is that we can just find some consistency, some working together," he said. Democrats say they heard both messages. "We ran on affordability, we won on affordability, and now it's our job to govern on affordability," said House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries on MS Now's Morning Joe. But here comes the difficult part. Democrats will hold Congress. Donald Trump still has the power to block their plans. The scale of the win was bigger than most forecasters expected, with at least seven Republican-held Senate seats changing hands. Behind the result was a striking mood: just 21% of Americans are satisfied with the direction of the country, even though the economy looks healthy on paper. Voters weren't looking at the statistics. They were looking at their grocery bills, electricity bills and the price at the petrol pump. In rural Texas, rising costs were even hurting Republicans in their own backyard. Sid Miller, the outgoing Republican agriculture commissioner, told me ranchers are getting $300 to $500 less for each head of cattle, while also facing record fertiliser costs. "They felt betrayed," he said. This was more than a blue wave. It was a vote about the cost of living. So what can Democrats actually do about it? Under the banner "Fighting for an Affordable America," Democrats say healthcare is their first priority. They want to bring back the extra financial help that made health insurance cheaper under the Affordable Care Act and reverse the cuts to Medicaid signed by President Trump in 2025. Next come tariffs and energy. Democrats want to scrap the president's import taxes, which they say add thousands of dollars a year to the cost of groceries, fertiliser and building materials. They also want to end the war in Iran, which they link to petrol prices averaging $4.18 a gallon, marking an increase of nearly 40%. Housing is next. Some Democrats want to build four million new homes over the next decade. On tax, they want to make billionaires pay more and increase tax credits for families with children. It's a long list. But how much of it can they actually deliver? Investor Ken Fisher, founder of Fisher Investments, puts it bluntly: "Congress can't get anything past a presidential veto. President Trump can't get anything he wants." The result, he says, is likely to be two years of relative quiet on the legislative and regulatory front. In other words, winning in Congress does not give Democrats a free hand. President Trump can still block legislation, and getting around a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate. For voters hoping for lower bills, that may be a disappointing result. They didn't vote for political deadlock. Take tariffs. Trump is unlikely to abandon a trade policy that is central to his agenda. Democrats will need Republican support if they want to change it. Bernard Yaros, deputy chief US economist at Oxford Economics, expects the average tariff rate on imports to stay around 10% for the rest of Trump's term. And there's another complication. Tariffs are bringing in more money for the government. Import taxes accounted for just over 1% of federal revenue in 2024. This year, they account for more than 5%. That growing contribution to government income, Yaros argues, will make tariffs "tough for a future administration to fully dismantle." Still, there are bargains to be struck. President Trump told CNBC he could work with Democrats on "many more things than people understand". Healthcare might be one of them. Yaros sees the possibility of a big political trade-off: Democrats agree to extend Republican tax cuts in return for restoring health insurance subsidies. But he doesn't expect a deal until late 2027, with the economic benefits arriving in 2028. That's a long time to wait for anyone struggling with bills today. Democrats could also turn up the pressure on businesses. Henrietta Treyz of consultants Veda Partners says Democrats will question companies that passed on the cost of tariffs to customers. After the Supreme Court ruling in February, she says, the question will be: "Did you turn around, take that tariff rebate, and then lower prices for consumers?" Companies will also be asked: "What did you get in exchange?" Democrats, she adds, will "pick and choose very carefully." In the Senate, Ron Wyden, the Oregon Democrat set to chair the Finance Committee, has summed up his approach in six words: "affordability for us, accountability for them." He says he will use the committee to "reassert congressional authority" over trade policy. Insurers, drugmakers and banks should expect to be called to explain themselves. And some of the biggest changes may happen closer to home. State governors and regulators have a say in electricity prices, while local authorities decide where new homes can be built. Democrats have won governorships in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, where the rising cost of electricity for data centres is already a concern. The hardest test may be something Democrats cannot fix with a new law. The price of petrol, diesel and fertiliser will depend heavily on what happens in the war with Iran. And forecasters disagree about what comes next. Oxford Economics warns that with the election over, further escalation "appears more likely," because petrol prices will no longer be as much of a political concern for the president. And here's the awkward part. If prices come down, Democrats may struggle to claim the credit. If they go up, they may share the blame. There is an immediate test, too. Government funding runs out after 11 December, and the chances of another shutdown look uncomfortably high. Democrats won the argument. Now they have to show they can make life cheaper. You can listen to an in-depth discussion about all these issues on a special edition of Business Daily's Power Players out soon.

title: Thatcher's Right to Buy split my estate. Now its days could be numbered
content: Growing up in a council flat in the 1980s and 1990s, my mum would often point out homes that tenants had bought from the council. You could usually tell just from looking. A plain wooden door had been replaced with something fancier. New windows had appeared. Sometimes there was a porch or pillars outside the front door. Those houses were bought under the Right to Buy scheme - arguably the most consequential housing policy of my lifetime. It was introduced in 1980, three years before I was born, when Margaret Thatcher's government gave council tenants in England the legal right to purchase their homes at a discounted price. Supporters welcomed the chance for working-class families to own their own home and build wealth. Critics argue it hollowed out the country's stock of social housing and contributed to today's housing crisis. Some of my neighbours "made a killing" from the policy, in the words of my mum. One bought an almost identical flat to ours in 1989 for £21,200, after receiving a discount of £18,800. Eight years later it sold for £54,500. Five years after that it changed hands again for £143,000. (Notably, the person who made the most money from that flat wasn't the original council tenant - it was the people who bought it afterwards.) But Andy Burnham doesn't like the policy. The Right to Buy scheme has seen various changes since its introduction in the 1980s, and Labour has weakened it significantly since coming to power in 2024. Then, in September, the prime minister told Labour's conference: "We will reform Right to Buy. Not taking the right away from anyone in an existing home, but removing it from new homes." This would help to keep council houses in public ownership "for generations to come", Burnham told delegates. He has previously compared trying to solve the housing crisis while continuing to sell social homes to "trying to fill a bath with the plug out". More than 40 years after its introduction, Right to Buy remains a debate about political values as much as housing policy, balancing the home ownership ideal against the desire to preserve social housing for future generations. Since 1980, more than two million homes have been sold through the scheme in England. In fact, about 40% of England's council housing stock has been sold through Right to Buy. Most of those sales took place in the early years, says Prof Rebecca Tunstall, a housing academic at the University of York and London School of Economics. At the time, Labour was vehemently opposed to Thatcher's plans. Yet many of its own voters went on to benefit from them. Labour now argues that not enough of those two million homes were replaced. Sir Keir Starmer's government restricted the scheme, including by heavily reducing the maximum discount that councils were allowed to give tenants. And now Burnham is removing the right to buy entirely from any new-build social home. The measures are included in a bill currently making its way through Parliament. The government says that before Labour's various restrictions on the scheme, England was projected to see a net loss of 26,000 council homes over the next decade. Now there will be a net gain of 18,000 homes over the same period, it calculates. This opens up a political divide: some opposition parties, like the Conservatives and Reform UK, say they would keep or even extend the scheme. For those who became homeowners, Right to Buy turned a dream into reality. Barbara Stevens, now 80, bought her two-bedroom council flat in Kentish Town, north London, through Right to Buy for around £35,000. Now mortgage-free, she estimates it could be worth between £600,000 and £700,000. "I've always wanted to own my own property," she says. Her friend Trevor Abrahmsohn believes her story demonstrates the success of the scheme. "If you want to condemn the poor to poverty, make them lifetime renters," he says. Those arguments were central to Thatcher's vision of a "property-owning democracy". Few people are more closely associated with Right to Buy than Lord Heseltine, who was the cabinet minister responsible for housing when it was introduced. When he and Thatcher launched the scheme in 1980, council tenants were offered substantial discounts to purchase their homes. A relative of mine whose parents bought their council home in Croydon told me it was the only time "anyone would ever give you a hundred grand for free". Even Housing Secretary Angela Rayner - part of the government that's restricting Right to Buy - bought and later sold her own council home for a profit. In 1980, Lord Heseltine described the scheme as the biggest transfer of capital wealth from the state to ordinary people. "It certainly was," he says now, almost half a century on. I ask him if, looking back, he would have designed the policy differently. "No," he answers. He thinks Right to Buy gave its beneficiaries an important asset. "People who bought their own homes made a great deal of capital gain," he says. But to its detractors, Right to Buy is responsible for many of Britain's housing woes. Prof Tunstall says the policy is partly responsible for making social housing scarcer, which meant more people competed for homes in the private rented sector, pushing up rents. Lord Heseltine says it was originally assumed that councils would use sale proceeds to support new housing. He acknowledges that did not happen after he left government. That failure to replace sold homes sits at the heart of the modern criticism of Right to Buy. For Molly Harris from the New Economics Foundation, it is "private landlords [who] are the real winners". Her think tank's research found that 41% of homes sold through Right to Buy are now privately rented out. "Homes that were built with public money, and with the aim of providing an affordable and secure path to home ownership, have since been turned into assets," Harris says. She says the shortage of social housing means more people need help with housing costs in the private rented sector, where rents are higher. So taxpayers are effectively paying twice: once to give a discount on the initial home; and then again, via housing benefit, when that home is rented out to someone who can't afford the payments. A former council home rented privately could now be valued at double, triple or quadruple what it cost when it was under local authority control. I put that criticism to Lord Heseltine, asking him whether the scheme has failed because some ex-council homes are now effectively being rented back to the state, at higher costs. He dismisses it as "rubbish", adding: "The scheme was wildly successful in spreading ownership across the country." According to Harris's research, the government spent more than £58bn between 2021 and 2025 "subsidising private landlords" through the benefit system. Newham Council says almost half of the 9,000 council homes sold under Right to Buy in Newham were later "flipped" into private rentals. The borough now has the biggest council house waiting list in the country. Last year, The Big Issue reported that Newham Council made a loss of more than £20m of taxpayers' money buying back homes it had sold just a few years earlier. The council said it was a quick way to provide new housing, and was a cheaper option than some alternatives. And some council tenants say they are not interested in buying their homes. Ruth Crabb has lived in her flat in Havering since 1997. "I wouldn't buy my flat because I didn't want it to go out of circulation, as social housing is for those who come after me," she says. But, she adds: "I don't judge anyone who bought their property with Right to Buy." Supporters of Right to Buy also argue that you can't appreciate the true value of the scheme by looking at numbers on a spreadsheet. The benefits of the policy extended for generations, they say, helping the children and grandchildren of those who bought homes. Research co-authored by Matteo Sandi, an economics professor at the University of Milan, looked at children growing up in areas where Right to Buy uptake was highest. He found better educational and economic outcomes, including higher GCSE attainment, greater chances of attending university, and increased earnings in adulthood. "What we find is that there is, in fact, a lasting benefit from growing up in an owned property," he says. He believes it's because ownership encouraged families to invest more heavily in their homes and neighbourhoods. One of my relatives backs this up. He tells me his parents were able to move elsewhere in the country, enjoy a better standard of living and finally afford things that had previously been out of reach. He believes Right to Buy transformed their lives. But Prof Tunstall argues home ownership is not the only route to a stable family life. "The critical things for safety and for children's development and for happy families are security and affordability," she says - and children can also get that from social renting, she thinks. Looking back, that resonates. When I was a child and my mum rented from the council, she knew what she would be charged every month. She knew we wouldn't suddenly be forced to move. My siblings and I knew we wouldn't have to change schools. At that point, in the 1980s, one third of houses in England were council-owned. When my mum became pregnant with me, it was safe to assume that a home would soon become available - and within about a year, one did. She moved out of my nan's and into her new council flat. The children I now meet through my work often do not have that certainty. Today, the average wait for a family-sized home in London is 27 years. Some children are moved repeatedly between hotels and hostels. Councils across England now spend £8m every day housing families in temporary accommodation. Sandi is careful not to present his findings as an unconditional endorsement of Right to Buy. "My take is the Right to Buy scheme was a good policy with a big limitation," he says. "More social housing should have been built." But curbing Right to Buy could take a long time to bear fruit, says Prof Tunstall. Scotland abolished its Right to Buy programme in 2016 and Wales followed in 2019 - but Prof Tunstall says it "hasn't made a huge difference" yet in those nations, because the changes are too recent. (Northern Ireland continues to operate a scheme similar to Right to Buy.) And deeper challenges will remain; Right to Buy is not the only culprit of Britain's social housing shortage, she says. Supply has also been reduced by council estate-clearance programmes, she says, which saw thousands of homes demolished from the 1990s. Like Lord Heseltine, she also blames decades of under-building: had governments continued to build at their 1980s rates, she argues, the sale of council homes might not have resulted in an overall loss of social housing. The housing landscape has also changed dramatically since 1980. Many councils transferred responsibility over council housing to housing associations, meaning they have lost the skills and expertise to build their own stock. More than 25 years later, I return to the street where I grew up. It looks much the same, although a few new front doors suggest more homes have been sold. My mum never took advantage of Right to Buy; she continues to rent a council flat on a small estate in south London. I ask her if she regrets that. She says she simply wouldn't have been able to afford it. I tell her that the flat she could have bought for around £20,000 would now be worth somewhere between £350,000 and £400,000. "You're kidding?," she replies. No-one in the 1980s could have known what would happen to house prices or the cost of living. But whatever people think about Right to Buy, there is broad agreement on one point: the problem was not necessarily selling the homes. It was failing to replace them. Additional reporting: Jade Thompson, Larissa Tairo. Top image credit: Getty. BBC InDepth is the home on the website and app for the best analysis, with fresh perspectives that challenge assumptions and deep reporting on the biggest issues of the day. title: Canada's federal budget includes billions for sovereignty and tackling homelessness
content: Prime Minister Mark Carney has taken advantage of an oil revenue windfall to include tens of billions of dollars in new spending in his second federal budget, which focuses on building national sovereignty and addressing the high cost of living. "That's what this budget does: it's the next big step in our action plan to make this country more independent, more sovereign," Carney said on Thursday. "It focuses on growth, on people and that sovereignty, so we can live our lives as we wish." The budget - titled Masters of Our Destiny - lays the groundwork for a Canada that is less reliant on the US for trade. It also aims to tackle the stubborn affordability crisis by promising billions to end homelessness and build new housing. The C$142bn in new spending over the next five years is thanks to better than expected revenues from oil prices bolstered by the Iran War. Canada's deficit is over C$50bn ($36bn; £27bn), with no path to balance. Despite new spending, the budget shows that Carney has kept his previous fiscal goals intact. The country still expects its GDP to grow modestly in the next year, outpacing all G7 countries except the US. Its unemployment rate, while unsteady month-to-month, is overall lower than last year. But as people continue to feel squeezed by inflation and unaffordable housing, pressure has been building on Carney to translate his major investments into relief for the average Canadian. And some sectors of the economy are feeling deep pain due to US President Donald Trump's tariffs on key Canadian industries, leading to thousands of job losses and uncertainty that has slowed business investment. Here is a breakdown of some of the key takeaways for the 2026 federal budget. One of the largest line items in Carney's second budget is an C$11.2bn commitment over the next four years to combat homelessness. This includes funding for supportive housing, mental health and addictions treatment. Statistics Canada reported last year that one in eight Canadian households have experienced a form of homelessness in their lifetime. The government will also boost a grocery benefit that is available to low-and-modest income Canadians, which is estimated to provide C$2,570 for a family of four within one year. Canada's opposition Conservatives have been pressing the Liberal government on cost of living, and have routinely accused the prime minister of spending too much time on foreign trade missions and not enough addressing kitchen table issues. There are signs that Canadians are struggling to make ends meet. Average hourly wages have not kept up with inflation, according to Statistics Canada. Food bank usage has hit record highs. The average price of a home in Canada has dropped around 22% in recent years, mostly due to a clamp down on immigration. But houses are still too expensive for many in Canada's major cities - namely Toronto and Vancouver. And like the rest of the world, the rising price of fuel has made everything - from gas to groceries - more expensive. After hitting record population growth in 2023, which was fuelled largely by immigration, Canada has scaled back its newcomer targets significantly. This includes a cap on international students and temporary foreign workers, which have been relied on by companies to ease labour shortages. The Carney government has previously said it will keep its permanent resident admission target to 380,000 people annually until 2028. Meanwhile, it will gradually reduce its temporary resident arrivals to 370,000. There has been pressure on Carney to increase some of those numbers. A report from the Royal Bank of Canada in September warned that "without immigration, the country's population would shrink to half its size by the turn of the century". On the other hand, the Conservative opposition has called on the government to further lower its targets. In the new budget, Carney has opted to keep immigration levels flat. A big focus of the Carney government has been reducing Canada's reliance on the US as a trade partner, while also helping cushion the blow from Trump's tariffs on its key sectors. Last year, it promised millions in backing for businesses working to develop new export markets. It also lowered Canada's marginal effective tax rate in a bid to stop businesses from moving to the US to escape tariff pains. This budget builds on that, including plans to support specific sectors hit by US tariffs like steel and forestry. The new funding was welcome by Canada's forestry sector, with the BC Council of Forest Industries saying in a statement that the support "comes at a critical time for workers". Since March 2025, the Carney government has set aside nearly C$44bn in support for workers and businesses hit by US tariffs, the budget notes. The budget states that "diversification will take time, given the scale and depth of Canada's economic relationship with the United States. But the shift is underway". Sovereignty is a big theme in Carney's second budget, which proposes funding different measures to strengthen Canadian identity - whether it be through the arts or in space. Canada is the only G7 country that does not have the capability to launch its own rockets. A line item in the budget looks to change that, with C$2.7bn earmarked to developing Canadian space technology and launch infrastructure. On arts and culture, Carney is promising a tax exemption on income that is made through "original and creative artistic works". The budget also sets aside C$32.2m over four years to establish a free national digital library for Canadians. It will launch with at least 200 titles with plans to expand in coming years. Carney had previously pledged to significantly boost defence spending to meet the Nato target of 5% of annual GDP by 2035. This year's budget provides some insight into where that money is being spent. That includes a marketplace, launched earlier this year, to sell Canadian-made drones. It will get a cash injection of C$2.3bn over five years. More funding will also go into support for Operation Reassurance, Canada's largest overseas deployment mission to deter Russian aggression in eastern Europe.

title: Second buyer makes rescue bid for Poundland as retailer faces collapse
content: A second buyer has made a rescue bid for Poundland as the discount retailer teeters on the brink of collapse, with thousands of jobs at risk. London-based Xyra Group has offered to pay off half of Poundland's outstanding debts - a key sticking point in takeover talks so far - immediately. The rest would be deferred. With Poundland close to collapse, US-based owners Gordon Brothers have already rejected a rival bid from an Irish property group which would have saved its 12,000 staff. Gordon Brothers said the business has faced years of instability and "remains challenged and vulnerable". Sources familiar with the offer said Xyra is offering to immediately pay off £12.5m of an outstanding £30m loan on Poundland's books. The offer came as Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds held crunch talks with Gordon Brothers about the future of the business, urging the investment firm to protect staff however possible. Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for £1 last June, committed at the meeting to prioritise offers which protect its shops and workers. The company said: "We are pursuing all avenues through the sale process to find a solution which protects as many jobs as possible and preserves value. Work continues at pace, engaging in active discussions on offers with interested parties." Xyra is offering to pay off a higher proportion of Poundland's outstanding debts than Martin Property Group, which previously submitted a bid that Gordon Brothers rejected. But doubts remain about the credibility of Xyra's offer, as there is little evidence they meet Gordon Brothers' tests, including whether they have the money and whether they would be good long-term owners of Poundland. Sources pointed to the appointment of Andrew Brode to Xyra's board as a sign of its credibility. Brode works for RWS - a company that provides AI solutions for businesses. Judith MacKenzie, head of Downing Fund Managers, told the BBC Brode is "well known and very credible" among small businesses in the UK. But she said there is "hardly any information" publicly available about Xyra. "So, although some of the people look good, I can't find any evidence to say that they've got the money to back it up yet," MacKenzie added. Gordon Brothers said: "Our intent throughout the comprehensive sale process has been to protect as many jobs as possible and preserve value in order to deliver the best available outcome for all the people, creditors and local communities who care about this business as much as we do." Both Reynolds and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have questioned why a deal for the future of Poundland has not yet been made. Though Xyra made an offer to take over the whole business, it is unclear whether it would keep Poundland together as its owner or break the company up. Several Poundland suppliers have said they would also go bust if the retailer collapses. Its founder Steve Smith said two or three thousand suppliers to the firm, those who solely work for Poundland, would be caught up in the collapse. He added that not only would Poundland's 12,000 staff be affected in that case, but potentially up to 30,000 overall.

title: Three ways the interest rate rise could affect you
content: Interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years - and it could be good and bad news for you. Here are three ways the increase to 4% from 3.75% could affect you. Rate-setters at the Bank make changes to interest rates to fulfil their role of keeping price rises at a steady level. Higher rates are meant to encourage people to spend less, reducing demand for goods and services and limiting price rises. This impacts businesses in two ways - less money to spend among their customers may mean they sell less, but also the cost of borrowing to invest as a company goes up. Many businesses, particularly small ones, have variable rate loans which are influenced by the Bank rate. Firms say higher rates limit their ability to offer new jobs and wage rises. Mitchell Barnes, founder and chief executive of Ryse 3D, which manufactures 3D parts for the defence and automotive sectors, said the "reality" of rising interest rates was to look at the cost of employees and people. That could include greater use of robots rather than workers. "It's going to cause issues with, I suppose, employment across all sectors for people," he said. "You're going to see reduced employment, more automation, more robotics being put into facilities, just in order to increase efficiency and make that money go further." The Bank rate - and where it is expected to go in future - has a significant impact on the interest rates customers are offered on savings products. So, if you're saving up for something quite expensive, like a holiday, or very expensive, like a home, then a rate rise could be good news. When interest rates were low throughout the 2010s, the returns for savers were poor, but borrowing costs were low too. The answer then and now, according to experts, is to make sure you move your savings to benefit from the best possible rates. Leaving your savings in an old account (a product not offered to new customers), rather than shopping around, can mean you are penalised for your loyalty. "Savers have endured years of unrewarded loyalty, with those leaving [a £20,000 cash pot] in closed accounts losing out on an extra £139 over the past three years compared to on-sale easy access accounts," said Rachel Springall, from financial information service Moneyfacts. She also said locking away your money for longer, with a fixed-term deal, is usually more lucrative. The other flipside is that renting while you save could get more expensive, because a rising Bank rate may well increase costs for landlords. The big losers from a rate rise are those who borrow money, and specifically those on variable rate mortgages. About 500,000 homeowners have a mortgage that "tracks" the Bank of England's rate. Any rise in the Bank rate means an increase in the monthly repayments on their outstanding loan. For a typical loan, the cost is going up by about £31 a month now the Bank has raised the base rate, but it depends on the size of people's loans. An additional 500,000 homeowners on standard variable rates (SVRs) must wait to see if their lender chooses to pass on any Bank rate rise. Typically, this would mean a £14 increase per month in repayments for a 0.25 percentage points rates rise. If you, like 87% of mortgage-holders, have a fixed-rate deal, then the payments will stay the same until the end of your current deal, which is usually two or five years. While monthly payments are not immediately affected by a rate change, future deals are. Lenders had already "priced in" the latest rate rise when quoting new deals. Expectations for the Bank rate into next year are crucial on what they offer next. The average rate on fixed deals are much higher now than was predicted at the start of the year. It means those remortgaging, possibly after the post-Covid boom in the housing market, are facing the prospect of higher mortgage payments. Some people have been choosing to move onto tracker deals instead, taking a view - including some risk - of the Bank rate not moving towards a series of further hikes.

title: The engine parts that 'fight the laws of the universe'
content: Every time you fly, an extraordinary feat of endurance occurs inside the aircraft's engines. Hidden from view inside the sleek outer nacelle are hundreds of little turbine blades that can shrug off enormous mechanical stresses and temperatures exceeding 1,500C. It is a true engineering marvel. And these hardy blades are not sculpted or cut from their material – they are grown. During the 1960s, engineers worked out how to take a molten metal alloy, cast it into the shape of a turbine blade, and then cool it very carefully from one end to the other over a matter of hours. A single crystal or grain of metal alloy forms during this process of gradual, delicate solidification. Like turning a cup of water into one big snowflake, of your own design, rather than a mini blizzard of many smaller snowflakes. "It's about as complicated as manufacturing gets," says Ben Fifoot, manufacturing engineer at Rolls-Royce, which makes turbine blades in the UK. "It's a real motivator to get out of bed in the morning." Only a handful of companies around the world can produce these single crystal turbine blades, and the process has been perfected end-to-end in just five countries, including the US and UK. Engine-makers continually vie for access to the technology. Rolls-Royce, GE and France's Safran are among the few firms that have perfected the process. In September, GE Aerospace announced it would acquire its turbine blade supplier for $11.75bn (£8.78bn). Neither company responded to BBC News' requests for comment but the move has been described as an effort to ensure supply of these critical components. Separately, in March, Rolls-Royce said it would invest more than £19m in its Rotherham blade casting facility. Turbine blade specialists continue to work on improving the capabilities of this little-known technology. All the while, China is desperate to prove that its engineers can produce turbine blades of the same quality as those in the West. Who will come out on top? "Demand for [turbine blades] is huge. So few companies have managed to do it, which does give it this kind of magical aura," says Bill Sweetman, an aviation industry writer and consultant. He suspects GE Aerospace's recent move is about securing reliability and predictability in the notoriously volatile aircraft manufacturing supply chain. But why is the single crystal casting process, which has been around for decades now, still so specialist? To grow one of these blades, asserts Fifoot, is to "fight the laws of the universe". This is because each molten blade would naturally cool into a solid object consisting of many small grains of metal alloy, all jumbled together. But you don't want a crumbly sugar cube, you want a perfect diamond. Getting a single crystal to grow into the shape of the blade instead isn't just a matter of cooling the molten version down slowly, the process also uses a bizarre trick called a pigtail. The pigtail is a small spiral at one end of the blade. Fifoot says that, at the beginning of the cooling process, this spiral "chokes" the flow of solidifying crystals so that just one takes over. A bit like a hairpin corner in an F1 race right before the finish line – one driver can take the lead here and go on to win. "Sometimes we need to play around with the number of turns or the angles on [the pigtail] to try and get more favourable grain," adds Fifoot. Once the blade is formed, this crucial but sacrificial spiral is cut off. Blades made by Rolls-Royce are used in aircraft engines including the Trent XWB-84, which powers the Airbus A350-900, and the Trent 1000 XE, for the Boeing 787. The single crystal is essential to ensure each blade's performance. Sometimes a blade doesn't cool quite as planned, for example two crystals form within it instead of just one, and the metal alloy must be reprocessed so that the manufacturer may re-use the material. Special ceramic coatings also protect blades from extreme temperatures inside engines. And another important feature is that blades are cast with tiny channels that allow a flow of cooler air to coat them in a kind of film while the aircraft engine is working. "The drive at the moment [across the industry] is currently to make those cooling passages really intricate," says Paul Withey, at the University of Birmingham, who formerly worked for Rolls-Royce. The more turbulent those little flows of cool air are, he explains, the more they will knock heat out of the surrounding, much hotter air. And blade-makers also seek to reduce the mass of these components as much as possible. "If we can take any weight out of it, you can run that engine more efficiently using less fuel – you can spin it faster and hotter," says Fifoot. Meanwhile, China hopes to become only the sixth country to master the whole technology chain for single crystal blade casting. A report in May quoted one engineer at the AECC Beijing Institute of Aeronautical Materials claiming that China now had a single crystal alloy "superior to or equivalent to the second-generation single-crystal superalloys widely used in Europe and the US". It costs less to make, too, apparently. But the West has a "huge advantage" over China given that the majority of commercial airliner production happens there, says Sweetman. Supply chains and the latest innovations are generally clustered in the West. Plus, Western manufacturers also have lengthy safety records under their belts. China must compete on practically every aspect of aircraft manufacturing – by no means just on turbine blades – in order to make serious in-roads. "You can definitely see that happening but it's a long, uphill struggle," adds Sweetman. Demand for aircraft is currently high, which is already straining various supply chains in the industry. That demand could grow higher still, suggests Withey. During the next few years, one of the two main aircraft manufacturers, Airbus and Boeing, could launch a new short-haul plane , he says. Then, the other would have to follow suit in order to remain competitive. "There'll be a bun fight," says Withey, over who gets to supply the engines and, by extension, those all-important single crystal turbine blades.

title: 'I was asked if I was a crier': Your worst job interviews revealed
content: Tiara Allen arrived on time to interview for a retail job. Her interviewer didn't. She waited for around 40 minutes in a shopping centre while the interviewer's co-worker called them "two or three times". When they finally showed up, Tiara says she was told it was because the meeting wasn't in the schedule. She needed work at the time, so took the job when she was offered it, but says she would handle the situation differently now. "I would not take a job if they took that long," she says, adding that she believed her treatment during the interview was a sign of how the firm tended to treat staff. Tiara is far from alone. She is one of many people who spoke to the BBC about their worst job interview experiences after we wrote about the one interview question that leaves you feeling uncomfortable . While those situations can be hard to deal with in the moment, they can also teach us a lot about the world of work. During an interview for an assistant at a book publisher in New York, Chas Edwards was asked a question he wasn't expecting. "I was asked for my first job if I was a crier," he recalls. Thinking the interviewer was being funny, Chas replied that he didn't cry. He was later told that this was why he got the job. "Her last assistant had cried – too often, I guess? – and she wanted someone who didn't cry. So she was being serious and I thought it was a joke," he says. It was a bad sign. Chas says it was "a terrible, terrible job with a miserable boss" and while he managed to make it through 13 months there without crying he was "crying inside". "I set the world record for working for this person. No-one had ever lasted three months with her before," he recalls. Despite all this, Chas says he is in some ways grateful the experience was so awful. "Because every job since then, even the bad ones, are not that bad," he says, adding that he can "cry anywhere now". Corinne Card also found herself floored when the first question she was asked in an interview for an administrative job was if she liked working with people. When she replied yes, she was told that the job wouldn't be for her and the interview ended there. "I don't know if it was a deliberate trap. Because who would answer 'I don't like working with people'?" Corinne Mills, joint managing director of Personal Career Management, says that it can be worth asking an interviewer to clarify any weird questions, perhaps by repeating the question back to them. However, if a line of questioning is really off-putting, she says it can also be a sign of what it's like to work there, saying that interviews are also about candidates judging the company. Meanwhile, other questions are not just annoying – they are illegal. Discrimination against a protected characteristic is against the law , meaning an employer cannot treat you less favourably based on your age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage, pregnancy, race, religion, sex, or sexual orientation. Employment lawyer Roy Magara says that women being asked if they intend on having children in an interview is a "quite common" kind of bias. He says he has also seen a case where an older candidate was told he didn't get the job after an interview because he didn't fit the "vibe" of a younger team. If you think these sorts of biases took place in your interview, Roy says you can send the company a subject access request to see how they discussed your application internally. Worst-case scenarios like these can make interviews feel very difficult, especially considering the control employers have over candidates. Euan Cameron, co-founder of hiring software Willo, says that even with this power imbalance it's important not to overthink what an interview is. "An interview is just a conversation between two people," he says. Of course, as in Tiara's case, it helps when both of those people show up.

title: Firms told to publish salaries in job adverts ahead of new law
content: Businesses should publish salaries in job adverts now, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is telling firms, rather than wait for a new law to come in that will force them to do so. The government is planning to make pay details compulsory in adverts, with legislation on the issue being brought forward "as soon as possible". It argues the change will help jobseekers, particularly those applying for their first job, and could help prevent pay discrimination. However, one industry group said setting pay was a complex process and regulating adverts was not always suitable. It comes a week after the UK's equality watchdog said employees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning . The Cabinet Office launched a consultation into pay and reducing discrimination in the summer, and the government said there had been "overwhelming support" for greater transparency, with 94% of respondents backing the move. "Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Burnham said. The government said the move was part of attempts to reduce the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - ahead of the final report of the Milburn Review into youth inactivity, which is due in the coming weeks. Publishing salary details upfront could "expose unjustified differences in pay, give workers greater confidence to challenge discrimination and prevent disagreements over pay escalating into disputes". The proposals are similar to measures being introduced in the European Union. Employers in Europe will have to disclose the initial pay or range for new roles, which must either be included in a published job advert or shared before an interview. According to data from UK jobs website Adzuna , 51% of the adverts on its site in September had salary information, but the proportion has been falling in recent years. Adzuna co-founder Andrew Hunter said being open about pay "should be the norm, not the exception". He added that employers who put a salary on a job advert "attract more applicants, and better-suited ones". Previous research from the CIPD , an industry body for human resources managers, has indicated that the public sector and charities are more likely to reveal pay information that private firms, while pay ranges were more common than specific salaries. But it found not all employers were "fully transparent", with pay ranges sometimes wider than £10,000. CIPD chief executive Neil Carberry said that while, in principle, giving salary details was "a good thing", in practice it was "more complicated". "There isn't always a single fixed figure, and employers will want to set pay based on a candidate's skills, experience and potential." Carberry added the process was complex, saying that drafting job adverts is "best left to good employer practice rather than government regulation". The government has said it will set out further details on what information will be required and how the legislation will be enforced "in due course". Last week, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), said publishing salaries in job adverts would be a "positive step". It also said bosses should be required to respond to questionnaires about colleagues' pay to cut pay discrimination. At present, employers do not have to respond to employee requests for salary information about their co-workers. The EHRC also said employers should be prevented from asking about current salary when offering a job to stop a history of discrimination from continuing. Employers in the UK are currently allowed to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, but applicants are under no obligation to tell them .

title: Drunk and dangerous e-bike riders face on-the-spot fines under crackdown
content: People riding drunk or dangerously on e-bikes – and those who jump red lights - could face on-the-spot fines under plans to curb anti-social behaviour. Firms which run shared e-bike schemes will also be expected to manage their fleets better and provide designated parking areas to keep pavements safe. They could also be required to take out insurance so people can claim compensation if they are hit by someone on a shared bike. It's part of a crackdown on what ministers called the "wild west" of e-biking – with a patchwork of rules across the country often leaving the streets unsafe for pedestrians. A consultation launched on Thursday sets out proposed national standards to make journeys safer for everyone and keep pavements clear, particularly for wheelchair users and families with prams. The first e-bikes were launched in Exeter in 2016 and arrived in London a year later, growing to become a popular commuter option. According to the Greater London Authority, 37 million trips were taken on dockless e-bikes last year – a third more than the previous year. Shared e-bikes - such as Lime, Voi, Beryl, Dott, Forest and Bolt - make short journeys quick and convenient. While some areas enforce rules that mean shared bikes can only be left in specific areas, others have looser rules. Under the government's proposals, local leaders will be able to license schemes in their area, allowing them to enforce minimum standards and better integrate e-bikes into existing transport networks. Measures could include requiring operators to have a parking plan and to manage fleet sizes and operating areas, so bikes aren't overcrowding streets. The consultation will also consider ways to tackle antisocial and illegal behaviour, to prevent users from riding shared cycles drunk, underage, or on pavements. There will also be clear consequences set out – such as fines - for this type of behaviour. The government is also consulting on whether local leaders should have extra powers, including setting fees and requirements for operators to share data to improve enforcement and journey planning. The consultation will last for eight weeks after which the government will draw up legislation to implement the changes. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the e-bike clampdown was a "small but important everyday fix" which would make streets safer. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said the government wanted e-bike schemes to "grow in popularity" but acknowledged they were "causing a little bit of nuisance at the moment". Asked how punishments for dangerous cycling could be enforced, Alexander said licensing rules could allow for fines but added: "What you can't do is legislate for every eventuality, you can't legislate for idiots." "The police enforce the rules of the road to stop cyclists when they are behaving recklessly but police have got a lot on their plate so individuals have to take some responsibility," she added. Bosses at Lime, Voi and Bolt all welcomed the proposals, adding that consistent standards being applied across the country would provide clarity and certainty for operators, riders and the general public. Mike Wordingham from the Royal National Institute for the Blind said 92% of blind and partially sighted people had been forced to walk into roads due to e-bikes blocking pavements. He welcomed the government's announced but warned that tackling rider behaviour would be "difficult" and said a locally-led approach shouldn't lead to "a patchwork of regulations and inconsistency in implementing them".

title: Faisal Islam: How high will interest rates go?
content: Interest rates have risen to 4% and the Bank of England has indicated there are more rises to come. The question is how many? There is a split on the rate-setting committee here. Three of the nine voting members referred to "rises" plural. One member voted for a bigger increase, to 4.25%. Three referred to just one more including governor Andrew Bailey. My read on this is that the expectation is for one more rise in February. Two and done, but it depends. It is painful for those on variable mortgages, but should not be seen as the start of a cycle of hikes. Predicting where interest rates will go is like throwing darts at a board that constantly moves around the wall, with expectations of how long the Iran War will last and its impact on the economy and prices lurching from day to day. At least there is no blindfold. The Bank's forecasts indicate inflation is heading to just under 5% next spring as a typical household energy bill surges by 27% in January to £2,150 a year. Why have they raised now? High and rising inflation risks a further cycle of self fulfilling expectations of rising prices. It hasn't been seen so far, however. The war has lasted for 9 months, and led to oil prices used in the forecast averaging $108 a barrel. And yet on the day they have announced the rate rise, the oil price is actually 13% lower than that having fallen in the run up and after the US mid term elections, reflecting expectations or guesses that President Trump will now retreat or deescalate from the Iran war. The other notable factor is that the UK economy is performing much better than forecasts and expectations. This is underlined by the Bank of England's latest forecasts. Growth has been 0.6%, and 0.5% in the first two quarters of the year. It is heading for 0.7%, the Bank said, between July and September, before slowing in the three months to the end of the year. Unemployment has stabilised, actually falling a little. Some of this has fed through into a better performing currency , with sterling at its highest level since the Brexit referendum, when measured against a basket of currencies. This can help rein in inflation by making imports cheaper. So, this is an unusual type of uncertainty. Even the expected further rise, probably in February next year is conditional on the war continuing. The Bank of England stopped waiting for President Trump's war to end today, but perhaps the Democrats' resounding victory in the US midterm elections will stop the inflationary wave? The Bank has thrown a tentative first dart, and there is probably another to come.

title: Thicker bacon and ditching breakfast. Wendy’s hopes a menu shakeup can revive sales
content: Wendy’s reported its seventh consecutive quarter of declining sales, prompting the company to reveal a turnaround plan while rejecting a massive takeover offer. Thursday’s earnings caps off a tumultuous period for the 56-year-old chain, which included hundreds of closures, leadership changes and slumping sales. Wendy’s has been battling a number of issues that hurt its bottom line, including consumers cutting back on dining out, higher beef prices and value offerings that aren’t bringing people in. Same-store sales at its US locations fell 5.7% for the third quarter ending on September 27. Wendy’s sales trails its chief rivals, including McDonald’s, which fell 0.2%, and a reinvigorated Burger King, who reported an 8.4% increase. The multi-year turnaround plan, dubbed “Dave’s Way” after Wendy’s founder Dave Thomas, will include improvements to the food, better marketing and expanded delivery. CEO Bob Wright on Thursday said that its “objective is clear: grow customer traffic and market share while strengthening restaurant profitability.” At the same time, the chain’s board announced that it “unanimously rejected” a $1.4 billion offer from a group of investors, including former chairman and largest shareholder Nelson Peltz, to buy Wendy’s and take it private. The company said the offer undervalues Wendy’s and its potential. “Our confidence rests firmly in Bob Wright’s proven track record of seasoned industry leadership, including restaurant business turnarounds,” said Art Winkleblack, Wendy’s board chair and a member of the independent committee, in a statement. Wendy’s new plan will improve the food, with a “fully refreshed menu” rolling out in 2027. Wright has previously criticized that the chain had prioritized cost savings over the quality of the food. The chain is starting with the ingredients – thicker bacon, bigger pieces of lettuce for sandwiches, creamier Frosty’s and upgraded salads. Wright said that the chain is also “removing lower volume items that add complexity in our kitchens.” One major part of the menu that could go away is breakfast, which Wendy’s launched in 2020 . The company is now making it optional for franchisees. Locations that have stopped selling it report better results during other parts of the day. “This option directly supports stronger restaurant economics, improves the employee experience and importantly allows operators to concentrate on the food offerings and day parts,” Wright said. Over the past several months, Wendy’s has shuttered nearly 300 of its 6,000 restaurants across the United States that were “consistently underperforming . This was the second wave of substantial closures within two years, part of the chain’s efforts to boost profits at nearby locations. In May, Wendy’s appointed Wright as its chief executive officer, ending a nearly year-long leadership drought after previous CEO Kirk Tanner left for Hershey after just 18 months with the chain. Wright’s record of growing sandwich chain Potbelly was likely seen attractive to Wendy’s board, considering same-store sales have fallen for six consecutive quarters. The new CEO was blunt during his first earnings call in August, saying the chain was “not performing at our potential.” Notably, Wendy’s let rival Burger King surpass it in US sales this year, knocking it down to the country’s third-biggest burger chain. “Our value proposition has slipped, and franchisee economics are under pressure,” Wright previously said. “I’ve seen this brand at its best, and I know we can fix these issues.” Wendy’s struggles have also adversely affected a major franchisee, Meritage Hospitality Group, which operates more than 300 US locations and partially blamed its bankruptcy on Wendy’s slumping sales. The franchise group said that its store-level earnings nosedived nearly 50% last year, citing rising beef costs, increased discounting and weak traffic. Wendy’s announced that it was planning acquiring “up to” 163 locations from the group, unless they receive a better offer. Wendy’s has unveiled transformation plans in the past, prompting an analyst on the call to ask what’s different about this version. Wright said that, compared to previous plans, franchisees are behind this one. “The restaurant business is deceptively simple to understand,” Wright said. “Writing a strategy that makes sense is the easy part. It’s unbelievably difficult to execute, and it requires that that execution strength across all disciplines.”

title: Musk bet big on keeping Texas red. What happens to his business empire now?
content: Elon Musk poured nearly half a billion dollars into the midterms to support Republican candidates, most to help Ken Paxton defeat Democrat James Talarico in the Texas Senate race. Talarico won. But it was the other Democrat upsets in the state, for governor and attorney general, that could cause bigger problems for Musk and his Texas-based companies: rocket and AI company SpaceX and electric car maker Tesla. Not only will he likely face greater regulatory scrutiny, but both candidates took direct aim at Musk and his businesses while on the campaign trail. “It’s less about the blue wave on the Senate or House side,” said tech analyst Daniel Ives, a SpaceX and Tesla bull, about what Tuesday’s election results mean for Musk. “It’s more with the Texas governor.” Democrat Nathan Johnson, who is replacing Paxton as Texas attorney general, said in July that, if elected, he would investigate whether SpaceX’s Starlink service was unfairly awarded grants designed to expand rural broadband. The internet service is SpaceX’s most profitable unit. And Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who unseated incumbent Greg Abbott, made opposition to data centers a major plank of her campaign. She has vowed to put a moratorium on new data center construction. Both Tesla and SpaceX have banked their future success on their AI efforts. SpaceX is planning major investments in new data centers in the next year, including the massive Colossal 3 to be built just outside of Brownsville, Texas. Unlike a lot of artificial intelligence companies, SpaceX earns a profit from selling time on its servers and cloud platforms to other AI companies. Hinojosa’s proposed moratorium would be a critical blow to its plans. “I mean, those Texas data center plans are a key part of Musk’s ambitions,” Ives said. He said that’s why SpaceX and Tesla shares fell Wednesday, both dropping more than 3%, even as many other tech stocks rose. Musk, the world’s richest person with a net worth estimated at about $898 billion, likely won’t sweat the money he lost backing Republicans, or even Wednesday’s decline in value for his shares. The bigger issue for Musk is an increased level of scrutiny, which he noted on his social media platform, X, on Wednesday. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk wrote, referencing his ultimate ambitions. Experts say lifting and operating data centers in outer space still face many hurdles. But even if it was possible, SpaceX may have to take off from a spaceport in Louisiana if Texas moves to limit launches. SpaceX has faced public criticism for the operation of its spaceport, “Starbase,” on Texas’ Gulf Coast. Some residents near the launch facilities have long expressed worries about disruptive sonic booms — which can be as loud as gunshots and register as small earthquakes — and collectively filed a lawsuit this year. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment about the lawsuit. But Musk has previously downplayed sonic booms, saying in a 2022 post on X that “storms and hurricanes that are far more serious than Starship launches.” Those resident complaints, however, could find a more sympathetic ear from Hinojosa compared to Abbott. (Hinojosa’s campaign did not respond to questions from CNN about her position on the spaceport.) Tesla also has a big operation in Texas, and its driverless “robotaxis” only operate in four cities in Texas and three cities in Florida. For comparison, rival Waymo, a unit of Alphabet, operates in 15 cities across the country. Local governments decide which vehicles, self-driving or otherwise, are allowed on their roads. “It would it would be a big blow if robotaxis faced more regulation,” Ives said. Tesla hasn’t listed profits or losses for its robotaxi service. But Musk has made it clear that Tesla’s future is selling rides in its robotaxis, not car sales. And a large part of Tesla’s evaluation is the expectation that its robotaxi service will eventually operate nationwide, Ives said. Ives also says Hinojosa’s threat to the AI industry goes beyond just SpaceX. Texas is a key to US AI development. The state has the most planned data centers in the country, according to research firm Cleanview, and is second only to Virginia for the number open or under construction. “Hinojosa is a known anti-data center politician and negative on the AI buildout which makes worries around the future of the datacenter buildout in Texas a real issue for tech investors,” Ives said in a note to investors Wednesday. “SpaceX stock will be under pressure.”
